title: MARTHA WAS SERVING JESUS—SO WHY WAS SHE BECOMING ANGRY?
paragraphs:
MARTHA WAS SERVING JESUS—SO WHY WAS SHE BECOMING ANGRY?
She welcomed Christ into her home, worked for Him, and tried to serve Him well. Yet somewhere between serving Jesus and resenting her sister, Martha lost sight of the very Person she was serving. Then Jesus said something every exhausted Christian needs to hear: “One thing is necessary.”
There is a frightening way to lose your peace without ever leaving the presence of Jesus.
You can still pray.
Still attend church.
Still serve.
Still give.
Still help people.
Still post Scripture.
Still carry responsibilities nobody else seems willing to carry.
Still genuinely love Jesus...
and slowly become angry at everyone who does not seem to be doing as much as you are.
That is what makes Martha’s story so uncomfortable.
Her scandal was not that she rejected Jesus.
She welcomed Him.
Luke tells us that Jesus entered a village and Martha received Him. Her home was open. Her hands were working. Her intentions appear honorable.
And yet, before the scene is over, the woman serving Jesus is irritated with her sister and questioning Jesus Himself.
Think about that.
She was doing something for Christ while becoming frustrated with someone sitting near Christ.
That can happen to us too.
And perhaps the most dangerous spiritual exhaustion is the kind that still looks like faithfulness from the outside.
You keep serving while something inside you quietly begins keeping score.
Who helped?
Who didn't?
Who noticed?
Who thanked you?
Who showed up?
Who left you carrying everything?
Who seems to have time to sit while you are always the one working?
Eventually the exhaustion becomes resentment.
And resentment starts talking.
Luke 10:40 gives us one of the most revealing sentences in the entire encounter.
Martha essentially asks Jesus, “Lord, do You not care that my sister has left me to serve alone?”
Notice where exhaustion has carried her.
The problem is no longer merely Mary.
Now Martha is questioning the care of Jesus.
“Do You not care?”
Those words are still alive.
They come from hospital corridors.
From exhausted mothers.
From fathers carrying financial pressure nobody sees.
From pastors who keep pouring while their own souls are running dry.
From caregivers.
From ministry volunteers.
From the believer who has prayed for years and wonders why heaven seems silent.
From the faithful person secretly thinking:
Jesus, don't You see how much I am carrying?
Don't You see who abandoned me?
Don't You see that I'm doing this alone?
Don't You care?
And Jesus does something beautiful.
He does not humiliate Martha.
He does not call her lazy, faithless, useless, or wicked.
He calls her name.
Twice.
“Μάρθα Μάρθα...”
“Martha, Martha...”
In Scripture, the repetition of a name can carry profound tenderness and urgency.
Not merely correction.
Relationship.
Martha is unraveling emotionally, and Jesus speaks personally to her.
Then He exposes what is happening beneath all that activity.
The Greek of Luke 10:41 says:
“Μάρθα Μάρθα, μεριμνᾷς καὶ θορυβάζῃ περὶ πολλά...”
“Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things...”
Two words deserve our attention.
“μεριμνᾷς” — merimnas — from μεριμνάω, carrying the sense of being anxious, worried, or deeply concerned.
Then “θορυβάζῃ” — thorybazē — conveying agitation or inner disturbance.
Jesus was not simply examining Martha’s schedule.
He was exposing Martha’s soul.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because the lesson is not:
“Serving is bad.”
It isn't.
Jesus Himself came not to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many.
Christian discipleship is not passive spirituality.
Love serves.
Faith works.
Compassion moves.
The Gospel produces hands willing to wash feet.
The problem was never that Martha had hands busy serving Jesus.
The problem was that the many things around Jesus had begun drowning out Jesus Himself.
Luke uses another striking word in verse 40:
“περιεσπᾶτο” — periespato.
Martha was being “distracted” or pulled away by much serving.
That is haunting.
Because you do not have to be distracted by pornography, greed, drunkenness, hatred, or obvious rebellion.
Sometimes you can be distracted from Jesus...
by what you are doing for Jesus.
Read that again.
You can become so consumed with preparing the table for Christ that you stop listening to Christ at the table.
You can become so busy defending Christianity that you stop behaving like Christ.
So occupied with ministry that prayer becomes mechanical.
So committed to helping everybody that bitterness begins growing toward the people who never help you.
So determined to keep the family together that your heart becomes angry at the family you are trying to save.
So busy building something “for God” that communion with God becomes the first thing sacrificed to keep it running.
And perhaps that is why this story hurts.
Because Martha is painfully relatable.
She was not serving a false god.
She was serving Jesus.
She was simply becoming consumed by “many things.”
Then Christ gives the sentence that cuts through the noise:
“ἑνὸς δέ ἐστιν χρεία.”
Henós de estin chreia.
“One thing is necessary.”

There is a textual variation among ancient Greek manuscripts here. Some witnesses have wording that can be rendered along the lines of “few things are needed—or one,” while others preserve the shorter “one thing is necessary.”
That variation should make us careful, not fearful.
Because the thrust of Jesus’ response remains unmistakable.
Mary had chosen the good portion.
And it would not be taken from her.
What was Mary doing?
Luke says she was sitting at the Lord’s feet and listening to His word.
Not performing.
Receiving.
Not proving.
Listening.
Not comparing.
Remaining.
Mary understood something Martha had momentarily forgotten:
Before Jesus wants the work of your hands, you need the life that comes from His presence and His word.
Christianity does not begin with what you can accomplish for Christ.
It begins with what Christ has accomplished for sinners.
That is the Gospel.
And this is where Martha’s kitchen leads us all the way to Calvary.
Because if Christianity were fundamentally about doing enough for Jesus, none of us could ever finish the work.
There would always be another plate.
Another obligation.
Another failure.
Another sin to compensate for.
Another spiritual achievement to chase.
Another reason to wonder whether God is finally pleased.
But Jesus did not come merely to recruit exhausted servants.
He came to rescue sinners.
At the cross, Jesus accomplished what Martha could never accomplish through service and what you and I could never accomplish through religious effort.
He bore sin.
He carried judgment.
He stood in the place of the guilty.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And He rose again.
The heart of Christianity is not exhausted humanity finally doing enough for God.
It is the Son of God doing what exhausted, sinful humanity could never do for itself.
That is why grace destroys our scoreboard.
You no longer have to make your usefulness your identity.
You no longer have to secretly measure your worth by how much you accomplish.
You no longer need somebody else's laziness to make your faithfulness meaningful.
You no longer need applause to prove your sacrifice mattered.
Christ sees.
Christ knows.
Christ is enough.
And when you forget that, even holy work can become heavy.
Perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You started serving because you loved Jesus.
Then somewhere along the road...
you became tired.
Then disappointed.
Then irritated.
Then quietly bitter.
Now you notice everything everybody else isn't doing.
You still smile.
Still serve.
Still say, “God bless you.”
But inside...
you are angry.
Maybe even angry with God.
“Lord, don't You care?”
And Jesus is not standing over you with disgust.
Listen closely.
“Martha, Martha...”
Put your own name there.
He sees beneath the anger.
Beneath the exhaustion.
Beneath the resentment.
Beneath the need to control everything.
Beneath the constant comparison.
And He is calling you back.
Not necessarily away from service.
Back to Himself.
Because Mary and Martha should never be reduced to a simplistic war between “workers” and “worshipers.”
The same Martha appears again in John’s Gospel.
When Lazarus dies, Martha goes out to meet Jesus and makes an extraordinary confession of faith.
She declares that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.
And later, in John 12, Martha is serving again.
Scripture does not tell us that Jesus commanded her never to serve another meal.
Serving was not the enemy.
Disordered devotion was.
Jesus was teaching Martha—and us—that service must flow from communion with Him rather than replace communion with Him.
Otherwise, something strange happens.
Your sacrifice begins demanding witnesses.
Your obedience begins demanding recognition.
Your service begins demanding that other people serve exactly like you.
And eventually you can become angry at your brother or sister while claiming your anger exists because you care so much about Jesus.
That is when we need Christ to expose us.
Maybe Mary isn't your real problem.
Maybe your spouse isn't.
Maybe that church member isn't.
Maybe that friend isn't.
Maybe the deeper wound is that you have been carrying “many things” without continually returning to the One who gives meaning to all of them.
And Jesus still says:
One thing is necessary.
Not one perfect performance.
One Christ.
Not one more achievement.
Christ.
Not more applause.
Christ.
Not proving that you are more faithful than everybody else.
Christ.
Not earning God's forgiveness through Christian busyness.
Christ crucified and risen.
Come back to His feet.
Come back to His Word.
Come back to repentance.
Come back to grace.
Come back to the place where you remember that before you were a worker in His kingdom, you were a sinner in need of a Savior.
Before you carried anything for Him...
He carried a cross for you.
And perhaps this is your moment to become painfully honest.
Have you been serving Jesus while resenting people?
Have you been helping everyone while secretly furious that nobody seems to help you?
Have you become so busy with Christian activity that your private life with Christ is starving?
Have you confused exhaustion with holiness?
Have you been trying to prove your value through usefulness?
Have you whispered Martha's question in your own language?
“Jesus... don't You care?”
He does.
The cross settled that question forever.
God's love is not demonstrated by giving you a life where you never become overwhelmed.
God demonstrated His love toward us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
So repent where resentment has entered.
Forgive where bitterness has grown.
Confess where pride has been hiding beneath “faithfulness.”
Stop treating people as competitors on a spiritual scoreboard.
And receive again what cannot be earned.
Grace.
Maybe your scandal isn't public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your scandal is that the person everyone thinks is strong has become spiritually exhausted.
You have served while empty.
Smiled while angry.
Encouraged others while wondering who would encourage you.
Quoted Scripture while struggling to hear God for yourself.
You welcomed Jesus into the house...
but somewhere in all the noise, you stopped sitting with Him.
There is grace for that too.
This is what Jesus does.
He walks into human messes and rewrites stories.
From resentment to surrender.
From anxiety to trust.
From performance to grace.
From distraction to devotion.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, don't hide behind another religious sentence.
Be honest.

And if Christ has already been healing you from performance, bitterness, burnout, or comparison, tell somebody what He has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to keep another exhausted believer from walking away.
Then think of one person who lives like Martha in this moment.
The mother carrying everyone.
The father nobody checks on.
The ministry worker who never stops.
The friend who is quietly unraveling.
The believer who loves Jesus but has become exhausted by “many things.”
Because there will probably be another day when the kitchen gets loud again.
Another day when responsibilities multiply.
Another day when somebody doesn't help.
Another day when resentment whispers, “Nobody cares.”
Come back and remember:
One thing is necessary.
We want this community to remain a place where Scripture confronts us, grace restores us, and Jesus Christ remains at the center.
Supporting Gospel work should never be presented as purchasing God's favor.
But supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one practical way believers choose to participate in helping biblical truth reach others.
The deeper reason to stay close, however, is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Scripture.
Conviction.
Encouragement.
Accountability.
Spiritual nourishment.
And continually being pointed away from ourselves and back toward Jesus Christ.
Invite someone else to follow.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because sometimes confession is where hiding begins to lose its grip.
“Jesus, bring me back to the one thing.”
Because someday the plates will be gone.
The deadlines will be finished.
The applause will disappear.
The accomplishments people praised will belong to yesterday.
And when all the “many things” finally fall from our hands, only one question will ultimately matter:
Did all our serving bring us nearer to Jesus—or did we become so busy carrying things for Him that we forgot to sit at His feet?
You can have Jesus in the house and still become distracted from His voice—so when the many things begin stealing your heart, come back to the One who carried the cross for you.
